CausalChain: Iron overload/injury -> Increased ROS production -> Lipid peroxidation -> Depletion of GSH due to compromised cystine uptake -> Activation of iron-dependent ferroptosis -> Hepatocyte injury and progression of liver disease; Upregulation of the transsulfuration pathway -> Increased cysteine synthesis -> Enhanced GSH biosynthesis -> Increased GPX4 activity -> Reduced lipid peroxidation -> Inhibition of ferroptosis
Hypothesis: Enhancing the transsulfuration pathway in hepatocytes mitigates ferroptosis by compensating for impaired cystine uptake and sustaining glutathione production, thereby protecting against liver injury in diseases such as NASH and potentially slowing progression to fibrosis and HCC.
Abstract: Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by lipid peroxidation, plays a critical role in liver diseases ranging from drug-induced liver injury to non‐alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). While cystine uptake via system Xc− is a primary route for sustaining glutathione synthesis and mitigating oxidative damage, hepatocytes possess an alternative, adaptive mechanism—the transsulfuration pathway—for generating cysteine from methionine. This review-based hypothesis proposes that enhanced activity of the transsulfuration pathway in hepatocytes can offset impaired cystine uptake, promoting glutathione biosynthesis and GPX4 activity to suppress ferroptosis. Augmentation of this pathway may therefore offer a protective strategy against ferroptosis-induced liver injury and slow disease progression in conditions such as NASH.
